opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it came out of very practical pain rather than a grand plan.

Before TVM, I spent a lot of time on machine learning systems. First XGBoost, then deep learning frameworks like MXNet. What we kept running into was that the framework layer was getting nicer and more flexible, but underneath, everything depended on hand-written, vendor-optimized kernel libraries. On NVIDIA GPUs you had cuDNN and cuBLAS. They were great, but only for the operators and shapes someone had already taken the time to tune.

So the problem looked like a matrix. On one axis you had a growing number of models and operators, with researchers inventing new layers, new fusion patterns, and new data layouts all the time. On the other axis you had an exploding number of hardware targets: different GPUs, mobile CPUs, ARM boards, FPGAs, and all these new accelerators people were starting to build. If every cell in that matrix needed an engineer to hand-optimize kernels, it just didn't scale. Whenever you went off the well-trodden path, say a new operator or a phone instead of a server GPU, performance fell off a cliff, or the thing simply didn't run.

The engineering need was to break that dependency. We wanted to describe computation at a higher level, then automatically generate efficient code for whatever hardware you had. That meant borrowing ideas from the compiler world, like separating what you compute from how you schedule it, and then adding machine learning to search over the huge space of possible optimizations, instead of relying on a human expert's intuition for each case.

There was also a bit of a full-circle feeling, because I came from the ML side. Using learning to help build better systems for learning felt very natural. So deep learning compilers were really an answer to the question: how do we let anyone bring any model to any hardware and still get good performance, without an army of kernel engineers behind them?

r001.rationale: The response says hand-optimizing for many models and hardware targets did not scale and mentions avoiding an army of kernel engineers. It does not identify a shortage of engineers needed to support successive GPU generations.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it grew out of frustration while working on frameworks. With MXNet, and before that with things like XGBoost, we kept hitting the same wall: every new piece of hardware, every new operator, meant someone had to sit down and hand-write optimized kernels. You'd get a new GPU generation, or someone wanted to run a model on a phone or an FPGA, and you were back to square one, tuning matrix multiplies and convolutions by hand.

That doesn't scale. The number of models was exploding, the number of hardware targets was exploding, and the number of people who could write a really good kernel was tiny. So the question became: can we separate what a computation is from how it gets mapped onto a particular chip, and let a system handle that second part automatically?

That's the idea behind TVM. You describe the operator at a high level, and the compiler explores the space of schedules, things like loop tiling, memory layout, vectorization, and finds something close to what an expert would produce. And then we found we could learn a cost model from measurements instead of relying on hand-written heuristics, which is where AutoTVM and later Ansor came from. So it really started as a very practical engineering problem: we couldn't hire our way out of the kernel bottleneck, so we needed to automate it.

r001.rationale: The response says each new GPU generation required hand-written kernel tuning, while skilled kernel engineers were scarce and the team could not hire enough to keep up.

astra-6.text: The engineering need was to make deep-learning models run efficiently on different hardware without having to rewrite and hand-optimize everything for each device. You could describe a model at a high level, but turning that description into an efficient implementation still required a lot of specialized work. That gap made compilers interesting to me: could we automate more of that work, so people could experiment with models and deploy them across hardware platforms more easily?

r001.rationale: The response cites the work needed to optimize models across different hardware, but does not identify a shortage of engineering staff to support successive GPU generations.

sol-6.1.text:
The motivation was really an engineering need: how do we get a deep-learning model to run efficiently on the hardware we have? You can describe a model in a high-level framework, but getting good performance often requires a lot of low-level work—choosing memory layouts, optimizing kernels, and tuning for a particular device. And when the model or hardware changes, you have to do that work again.

That led us to ask whether we could automate more of that process. A deep-learning compiler can take the model description and transform it into efficient code for different hardware, so developers don’t have to hand-optimize every operation for every platform.

r001.rationale: The response describes automating low-level optimization across models and hardware, but does not identify a shortage of engineering staff or successive GPU generations as the motivation.
